en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Acelaka-vagga 48.
The Training Rule on Troops on Parade.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had set out with his army.
The group of six monks went to see the mobilized army.
King Pasenadi of Kosala saw the group of six monks coming from afar.
Having seen them, he had them summoned and said this:
"For what purpose have you come, venerable sirs?
"We wish to see the Great Kings."
“Venerable sir, why do you look at me, who delights in war?
Should not the Blessed One be seen?
Thus people complained, grumbled, and spread it about.
“How is it that the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, will come to see an army on active service?
It is a loss for us, it is a misfortune for us, that we must come to the army for the sake of our livelihood and for the sake of our wives and children.
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and lamenting.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the bhikkhus of the group of six go to see an army on active service? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that you went to see an army on active service?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, go to see an army on campaign? …”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
‘If any monk should go to see an army on active service, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu’s maternal uncle was ill in the army.
He sent a messenger to that bhikkhu, saying:
“I am ill with the army.
May the venerable sir come;
I desire the venerable sir’s arrival.”
Then it occurred to that bhikkhu: “A training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One: ‘One should not go to see an army on parade.
Yet this maternal uncle of mine is ill in the army.
How, now, should I proceed?”
He reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to go with an army for such a reason.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, should go to see an army on active service, except for a legitimate reason of that kind, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however:
Whoever is such a person … [and so on] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is what is intended by the term “bhikkhu” in this context.
"Deployed" means that the army,
having departed from the village, has either encamped or is on the march.
"Army" means:
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
An elephant consists of twelve men; a horse, three men; a chariot, four men; and infantry consists of four men armed with spears.
If he goes for the purpose of seeing them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Wherever he stands and sees [her], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Having left the range of sight, if he sees her again and again, there is an offense of expiation.
Except when there is such a reason.
Except when there is such a reason.
If he goes to see those who have been mobilized while perceiving them as mobilized, except when there is such a reason, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he goes to see those who have been mobilized while being uncertain of it, except when there is such a reason, there is an offense of expiation.
If he goes to see one who is on military service while perceiving him to be on military service, except when there is a corresponding reason, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he goes to see each individual, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Wherever he stands and sees [them], it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, having left the vicinity of sight, he looks again and again, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] is not engaged in military service but he perceives them as engaged, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not engaged in military service but he is uncertain [of it], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he perceives one who is attached as being attached, there is no offense.
There is no offense if,
while standing in the monastery, he sees [them].
If someone comes to the place where a bhikkhu is standing, sitting, or lying down,
or if he sees him while walking along the opposite path—
on account of such a condition.
In times of distress,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The eighth training rule concerning troops deployed for battle is finished.
